title: The speck and the plank (Matthew 7:1–5)
hook: judge not; take the beam out of your own eye first

segments.voice: Yesterday, Solomon, outdressed by a wildflower. Your line was today is enough: no borrowing tomorrow's trouble.

Someone in the group chat says something, and before you've finished reading it you've already written the review in your head. Tone-deaf. Typical. Who does that? It's fast, it's easy, and honestly, it feels a little good. Now Jesus, still on the hillside, turns from worry to this, with a picture so absurd it's meant to make you laugh: a man with a whole wooden beam sticking out of his eye, leaning in close to help his friend with a speck of sawdust.
screen: `THE REVIEW IN YOUR HEAD.` → `A BEAM IN THE EYE.` → `A SPECK OF SAWDUST.`

segments.voice: It opens with one of the most quoted lines in the Bible, in the King James: "Judge not, that ye be not judged." Then the reason: "For with what judgment ye judge, ye shall be judged: and with what measure ye mete, it shall be measured to you again." The ruler you use on other people is the ruler that gets used on you. Then the picture: "And why beholdest thou the mote that is in thy brother's eye, but considerest not the beam that is in thine own eye?" A mote in Greek is a karphos, a tiny chip, a bit of straw or sawdust. The beam is a dokos, a roof timber, the kind that holds up a house. Mark calls Jesus a tekton, a carpenter or builder, and this sounds like a builder's joke: the biggest piece of lumber in the shop, jammed in your own eye, while you squint at your friend's splinter. Judge not doesn't mean never tell right from wrong. Verse six asks for discernment, and verse five ends like this: "Thou hypocrite, first cast out the beam out of thine own eye; and then shalt thou see clearly to cast out the mote out of thy brother's eye." Then. After. The speck is real, and helping with it is allowed. But the order matters: first, your own eye. The Greek word hypocrite meant a stage actor, someone playing a part; here, the part of the judge. And there's a quiet mercy in it. When you've just wrestled with your own beam, you tend to be gentler with someone else's speck. You know how it feels to have something in your eye.
screen: `JUDGE NOT.` · `A CHIP AND A ROOF BEAM.` · `THEN SHALT THOU SEE CLEARLY.` · `THE PLANK FIRST.`

segments.voice: Bring to mind someone who has irritated you lately, and name the speck: what they did. Then gently ask one question, not to beat yourself up, just to look: is there anything like that in me? Maybe a plank, maybe a splinter, maybe nothing; sit with whatever you find, and if you pray, you can ask for clear sight.
Dokos, the Greek word for a roof beam, the biggest piece of lumber in the shop. A chip of sawdust in their eye, a roof beam in mine, and the beam comes out first.
Your line: the plank first. Then you can see clearly enough to help. Until tomorrow.

howItsDone: Many Christians examine their own conscience before correcting anyone else, and some churches build a quiet moment of self-examination into worship before confession or communion.

notes: 'The Gospels call Jesus a builder' rests on tektōn (Mark 6:3; cf. Matthew 13:55), usually translated carpenter; builder or craftsman is a common gloss. Confirm the wording.
hypokritēs as stage actor: standard lexical note.
'judgment' here is the KJV (1769) spelling in the quotation; the validator forbids British 'judgement' outside quotes, so the script uses judgment throughout.

Audit (wider sample): 'three famous words' was wrong (Judge not, that ye be not judged is seven words); 'the Gospels call Jesus a builder' narrowed to Mark's tekton, carpenter or builder; cut the stock lines 'here's what people often miss' and 'Christians have long heard'.
